claim: The same paper says digital payments 'can potentially moderate' the effect of income on currency demand and lower the currency-to-deposit ratio over time

claim: The paper reports the CiC-to-GDP ratio peaked at 14.4% in 2020-21 despite rapid growth of digital payments, and digital retail payments (UPI-led) grew at 51% (volume) and 27% (value) a year over 2016-17 to 2022-23
source: RBI Occasional Papers Vol 43 No 2 (2022), 'Cash versus Digital Payment Transactions in India: Decoding the Currency Demand Paradox' (S. Awasthy, R. Misra, S. Dhal; accepted 23 Jun 2023)
note: 'Currency demand paradox': cash and digital rise together

claim: The paper says digital payments are substituting transactional demand for cash but the store-of-value and precautionary motive for cash remains; use of cash at PoS fell to 27% in 2022 from 71% in 2019 (figure the paper cites from FIS 2023)

claim: Effect of cards on the currency-deposit ratio is THEORY: a card payment debits one deposit and credits another, so if it replaces a cash payment the public holds less cash (cdr falls) and the multiplier rises; credit-card use does not itself change reserves. This is our reasoning, not a figure
source: Our reasoning from the formula (BUL note 12) and the RBI paper's finding
note: Label on screen as reasoning. Counter-evidence: cash still rises with income and precaution (-03, -04). Official data on cdr over time not read (-11)
